sent:
You’re asking new users to (1) create/register an object in TapMint, then (2) request LayerLock verification; verifiers face a gated, manual approval flow. That’s a lot to ask before someone has seen the payoff, which explains “traffic but no sales.”

Do this next (low‑lift, high‑impact):
- Split intent: two single‑promise pages — “Get an object verified” and “Become a verifier.” Each page exists to win one action.
- Show the payoff first: link a real sample trust record on the verification page, and a real verifier profile on the verifier page. People commit faster when they can picture the outcome.
- Make the 2‑step explicit with one CTA: “Start verification.” If the object isn’t in TapMint, route to Step 1, then return to Step 2 with state preserved. The UX can be two steps; the promise should feel like one.
- Answer the scary questions in the first screen: what you’ll get, what’s required (docs/ownership proof), and typical review time. Put this above the fold; move everything else down.
- Count what matters: track and optimise to “verification request submitted” and “verifier application submitted,” not clicks or page views. Budget and effort follow those two numbers.

Mini‑checklist: “Get an object verified” page
1) Headline mirrors the first doubt (“Will my buyers be able to see and trust this?”) — followed by a 3‑item payoff list.
2) First screen blocks: What you’ll get; Requirements; Time to complete (Step 1 + Step 2).
3) Primary CTA repeated (“Start verification”). Secondary: “See a sample trust record.”
4) Objections row: privacy of data, cost/fees, proof of ownership — each answered in one line with a link to docs.
5) Remove detours: keep nav minimal; put docs/help in the footer.
6) Instrumentation: fire “start_verification” and “submit_verification”; pass through UTMs.

Mini‑checklist: “Become a verifier” page
1) Lead with value to verifiers (public, portable reputation) and how tiers work (self / expert / industry) in one graphic.
2) Eligibility checklist and typical review timeline, before the form.
3) Proof: link a real verifier profile and a sample trust record they signed.
4) Inline application form (no extra click); save state.
5) Track “start_application” and “submit_application” as your success events.

Why this works: when we did the same pattern for a B2B client (Ledgerly), cost per booked demo halved; the winning page opened with the blunt question buyers asked first.

If useful, I can turn the above into a one‑page wireframe for the verification page so your team can build from it.
